items.title: When Writers Lose Faith in Free Speech
items.description: On Thursday, the Atlantic staff writer George Packer delivered the Newark Public Library’s annual Philip Roth Lecture. This article is adapted from his remarks. P hilip Roth’s chosen vocation was the novel, and he practiced it almost nonstop for six decades with a monkish devotion. In his hands it became a thing of explosive invention, wildly comical and intensely serious. The critic Lionel Trilling wrote: “The most effective agent of the moral imagination has been the novel of the last two hundred years.” Roth’s readiness to experiment and provoke expanded his readers’ moral imagination—their ability to see beyond the appearances of their lives to the deeper reality. The reign of the novel has coincided with the centuries of democracy. I don’t think this is a complete coincidence, because no other literary form has such plasticity and variety; no other genre is so concerned with the moral struggles of individuals amid the social forces that constrict or enlarge their humanity. If democracy is the political system that allows the fullest human flourishing, the novel is the literary form that most fully cultivates our understanding of human possibility and tragedy and endurance. In 1959, 25-year-old Roth published a short story called “Defender of the Faith” in The New Yorker , just ahead of its inclusion in his first book, Goodbye, Columbus . Some Jewish readers strongly objected to the story’s caustic portrayal of a Jewish character. This was the start of Roth’s career-long embattlement with critics high and low. A certain Rabbi Emanuel Rackman, the president of the Rabbinical Council of America, complained to the Anti-Defamation League: “What is being done to silence this man? Medieval Jews would have known what to do with him.” Young Roth shot off a letter to Rackman: “He who criticizes must be silenced—that is a terrible tenet to have to live by, Rabbi, and I should imagine even more terrible to a spiritual leader.” Writers work in the creative tension between freedom and attachment. They have to maintain an inner distance from external demands, including the demands of politics; at the same time, they aren’t excused from the responsibilities of being a human and a citizen. They need to be left alone, but they can’t escape the world. Much of Roth’s work conveys the tug of this social awareness, even or especially in revolt against the duties it imposes. He was also fierce on behalf of freedom, and not only his own. He edited Writers From the Other Europe so that work by Milan Kundera and other Eastern Europeans could bypass the Communist censors and be made widely available to English-speaking readers. When the Iranian regime sentenced Salman Rushdie to death, Roth had him to dinner at his London flat, accompanied by half a dozen security officers. Perhaps because Roth’s own need to write was an unstoppable, nearly biological drive, any attempt to silence a writer awakened his primal rage—and woe unto the Rabbi Rackmans of the world. When it comes to threats to free expression, we usually think of government censorship. The current occupant of the White House, more than any president in my lifetime, is trying his best to be the grand inquisitor. He’s carried on a relentless campaign of legal actions and verbal attacks against journalists, broadcasters, comedians, immigrants with unpopular views, and just about anyone who criticizes him. His administration has allowed major media organizations to be bought up by his cronies and merged into near-monopolies. His executive orders have barred hundreds of words from official use. His Pentagon purged 381 books from the Naval Academy library, including Henry James and Sexuality (surprisingly popular with midshipmen). We expect governments to try to restrict speech. It isn’t in the nature of power to let offending views go undisturbed. For the past decade, we in the West have been preoccupied with the divisive effects of the propaganda and lies that free people avidly consume on social media. But reporting in countries such as Ethiopia, Afghanistan, and Myanmar always reminds me that old-fashioned repression didn’t end with the 20th century. Publishing a poem or story can still bring the risk of jail or worse. The threat comes from police and vigilantes, and the red lines are kept dangerously unclear. Burmese poets invent an elaborately coded language of metaphors to get their social criticism past official censors who scrutinize every word. I’ve never heard the case for literary freedom so passionately made as in the rain-soaked streets of Rangoon. [ From the April 2021 issue: The relentless Philip Roth ] Fortunately, in our country we have a First Amendment, and not even this American president can throw us in prison for what we say and write and read. But free speech depends on more than the law. It needs a culture of free expression—a set of widely shared habits and expectations that guide daily life, an ability to tolerate disagreement, a willingness to listen even, or especially, when we don’t like what we hear. The First Amendment stands there like a block of stone against the efforts of would-be government censors, but a culture of free expression is a delicate thing that has to be trained and tended. It can bloom and fade. It lives or dies in the inner recesses of our minds, releasing or smothering thoughts and words regardless of the protections of the First Amendment. In a late essay, George Orwell wrote, “If large numbers of people are interested in freedom of speech, there will be freedom of speech, even if the law forbids it; if public opinion is sluggish, inconvenient minorities will be persecuted, even if laws exist to protect them.” In other words, a culture of free expression is up to us. I want to explore why ours seems particularly weak. One of the reasons is coming from inside the house. I f Roth were still with us at 93, he would find that the censorious rabbis, commissars, and mullahs have become writers. This is a time of promiscuous boycotts, rampant deplatformings and depublishings—books removed from store shelves, canceled before publication, withdrawn from sale as if we had gone back to the age of medieval heresy-hunting. Except now, instead of being hoisted by the strappado or bound to the rack, heretics are disinvited from conferences and review-bombed on Goodreads. I’ve had a front-row seat at this literary auto-da-fé—and I admit that my close-up vantage might distort my view a little. Shortly after October 7, 2023, I joined the board of the century-old free-speech writers’ organization PEN America. My timing was perfect: A pressure campaign by well-known writers had just begun against PEN and its leader for their insufficient zeal in condemning the war in Gaza. When, rightly or wrongly, PEN failed to say what its critics wanted to hear, they launched an aggressive boycott of the organization’s two premier events, its literary-awards ceremony and literary festival. Because I was new, it took me a little while to realize that the purpose of the boycott wasn’t to push PEN into a dialogue or allow writers to make their views known. The purpose was to flex enough cultural power to force the cancellation of the events; if possible, to destroy PEN America. The boycott achieved the first goal and nearly achieved the second. I also learned that a successful campaign doesn’t depend on broad ideological agreement. A few true believers can build up a critical mass of support by applying heavy pressure through networks of friends and professional connections—convincing them that refusing to join would be morally wrong, or just not worth the trouble it would cause them—and recruiting enough joiners that the remaining holdouts are isolated and risk social censure. Under this pressure, a well-known writer called me to ask whether he should drop out of the PEN festival. He was worried about optics—because of the boycott, his panel might be down to a couple of white writers. Call me naive, but I still thought of writers as fairly independent-minded people who didn’t like to obey what D. H. Lawrence called their “mob self,” who were unwilling to be coerced by the crowd, ornery when it came down to the right to speak and hear, even a bit vain when given the chance to stand on their own. I urged my friend to stay on—but as we hung up, I could tell which way the wind would blow him. Each big-name departure generated others, until the exodus became a stampede and the events were finally canceled because of lack of participants. This sad experience was a revelation: Writers turn out to be just as susceptible to peer pressure and social stigma as other people—maybe more so. PEN America survived, barely. With new leadership, the organization went through another, related crisis. The trigger was again the Middle East. Last year, PEN published a long, detailed report on the cultural destruction of Gaza by Israel: the heritage sites, museums, libraries, and universities wiped out; the hundreds of journalists, writers, and artists killed. Then, this past summer, the organization published another document: This one dealt with the growing exclusion of Israeli, and even some Jewish American, writers from literary life. The piece didn’t try to prove a coordinated campaign of discrimination, but it described a hostile climate in which editors are reluctant to sign or even read work submitted by these writers and their agents, novelists are told to downplay Jewish characters and themes, and bookstores and festivals vet these writers for signs of “wrongthink.” The Pulitzer Prize–winning biographer Benjamin Moser exulted to The Wall Street Journal : “Zionism is out of fashion in the publishing world, and it’s not ever going to be in fashion again.” None of this is surprising. After all, more than 7,000 literary professionals have signed on to a global boycott of Israeli cultural institutions, including of individual writers and publishers who don’t adequately affirm their support for the Palestinian cause. It would have to be a pretty incompetent boycott not to create a chill. These two documents—one on cultural destruction in Gaza, the other on the exclusion of Israeli and Jewish writers—demonstrate why we need a group that’s committed to free expression regardless of political pressure. I don’t know of another organization that has done this work in showing the effects of this terrible war on culture across the lines of conflict. And yet, strangely enough, PEN America has become a pariah to many writers. The Gaza report didn’t get much attention; perhaps PEN’s boycotters already had what they wanted. But when the second piece appeared, it lit a small conflagration. PEN’s new board president, a novelist, immediately resigned . Several board members followed him out. The now-ex-president began to denounce the organization, saying that it should never have published the piece and calling it “unethical.” His complaint was that the document would harm the Israel boycott by giving ammunition to its critics, including American politicians who have sought to ban it as discriminatory. I’m opposed to laws that criminalize boycotts, but I’m also against suppressing the truth just because it might hurt a cause I support. The ex-president argued that a cultural boycott is a form of protected speech—and it is. But let’s not kid ourselves: Its purpose is to ostracize and ultimately silence disfavored writers. It is incompatible with a culture of free expression. [ From the May 2020 issue: Philip Roth’s terrible gift of intimacy ] So this is where we are: The leader of a free-speech writers’ group quit because it defended the free speech of writers. A number of confused friends called to ask me what the hell was happening. I did my best to explain, but honestly, by now I wasn’t surprised. This was no longer a man-bites-dog story. To PEN’s ex-president and others like him, literary freedom was never the real concern. What mattered was whether PEN helped or harmed their political cause. I’ve learned the hard way that writers can’t always be counted on to support the freedom of other writers—that sometimes they’re the last people to count on. The principle that makes their life’s work even possible no longer seems to carry the force of belief. The question is: Why? T he answer has something to do with politics—with an idea about the role of the writer in politics, and the role of politics in writing. We live in an intensely political time, and unless you’re making a huge effort to ignore the world around you, your mind is saturated with existential elections, partisan hatreds, historic corruption, wars and war crimes, global apocalypses, and the poisonous nature of the very information you’re consuming. The future of democracy and maybe humanity is at stake every day. It’s natural for conscious people to speak out, and writers especially feel they have an important role to play. At least since Zola defended Dreyfus, in times of crisis, writers have given their names to political causes and tried to move others to do the same. They feel that their work is an expression of their moral values, and they want to put that status to more direct use than sitting all alone in the cloudy realm of truth and beauty. Politics today seeps into everything, from pet-food choices to tampon brands. At the same time, literature is at risk of disappearing—or at least becoming the eccentric taste of a small elite, like opera. Philip Roth anticipated this back in 2004, when he said, “I don’t think in 20 or 25 years anyone will read these things at all. I think there are other things for people to do, other ways for them to be occupied, other ways for them to be imaginatively engaged, that are I think probably far more compelling than the novel, so I think the novel’s day has come and gone.” Right on time, we’re now told that we are becoming a “postliterate society,” we are entering “the new Dark Ages,” we have reached “the end of reading.” The percentage of Americans who still read at least one book annually has become as familiar an indicator of national decline as the Gini coefficient of economic inequality, or the life expectancy of non-college-educated white people. So one reason some writers feel justified in silencing others for political reasons might be the declining value of writing itself. Politics has never seemed more urgent, while literature has never seemed more marginal. If I can strike a blow for human rights and justice by shutting down a writer whose country is waging a brutal war, why would I let an abstraction stop me? (And I won’t pause to ask what good I’m really doing, other than for my own moral hygiene.) For example, the Pulitzer-winning New York Times columnist M. Gessen criticized the PEN piece on Facebook, essentially saying that its findings about Israeli and Jewish writers are exaggerated, irrelevant, or untrue—and if they are true, all the better. Gessen argued that no one would expect the writings of Heinrich Böll to have been published while he was a German soldier during World War II, or the work of a Russian writer who’s silent about the war in Ukraine to be made available in the West. Shouldn’t the same go for Israeli writers while Palestinians are being killed in Gaza and the West Bank? I won’t get into the business of weighing the Holocaust, Ukraine, and Gaza on the scales of historic crimes. What interests me is the role of literature at such a moment. An Israeli writer named Mikhal Dekel, replying to Gessen, spoke about the need to make room for writing that doesn’t fall into clear ideological categories—that might use an indirect or ironic style. Dekel herself is writing a book about the complex lives of Arabs and Jews who reside in the same building in Haifa. She invoked the South African novelist J. M. Coetzee, who was criticized for not taking public positions on behalf of the anti-apartheid movement, but whose novels, both realistic and allegorical, brilliantly portray the psychology of oppression. Gessen’s answer got to the point: “Now may not be the time for such literature. Not while the genocide is continuing and while the majority of people with those complex predicaments support it and tolerate it … Now, I think, is a time for laying down basic moral coordinates. The time when readers outside of Israel are ready to start filling in the many shades and colors of the grid will come later.” When the time comes, presumably Gessen will let us know. But while we wait, it’s worth thinking about the phrase “laying down basic moral coordinates.” It seems to describe writing that takes a clear position and compels a simple response. I believe that there’s a place for such literature. We shouldn’t make a fetish of ambiguity and disinterestedness that would oblige us to cancel Hard Times and The Grapes of Wrath . When James Baldwin attacks Richard Wright for writing a protest novel that denies the humanity of its protagonist, I nod along—but I would much rather reread Native Son than Giovanni’s Room . The intensity of Wright’s vision of injustice makes the crudeness of his characterization less important. There’s value in a literature that compels its own time to see the truth about itself. No one can doubt where Darkness at Noon and 1984 stand on totalitarianism. Yet Gessen’s “basic moral coordinates” make me uneasy—and not just because they’re offered as grounds for excluding certain writers. Something about the exhortation puts me on edge. It feels like the pressure of a hand on my back, gently but firmly pushing me toward foregone conclusions and absolute truths, when in fact the place where politics and literature meet is fraught with risk. Trilling called this place “the dark and bloody crossroads.” A lot of bad politics and bad books are buried there, or else emerged from the encounter damaged and diminished. At this intersection, politics often becomes what it rarely is or can be, a simple contest between right and wrong, while literature approaches a form of propaganda that makes artistic integrity impossible by requiring distortions and lies. [ From the April 2012 issue: Roth v. Roth v. Roth ] Entering the zone of politics seems to give writers a license to forget everything they ever knew about human complexity. Politics is the one place where life can be the morality tale that they’d never accept in a work of art. Social reality is reduced to an open letter with all of the right signatories, written in a tone of high righteousness—politics as an extension of personal conscience: “Here I stand. I can do no other.” The really dangerous temptation is to become a prophet—once writers let that happen, they stop being writers. Thomas Mann, who in his later years became a tireless public speaker for democracy and against fascism, was aware of the danger: “The political moralizings of an artist have undeniably something comic about them. Moreover his propaganda for humanitarian ideals must inevitably bring him closer than close to the platitudinous.” And when politics enters a literary work, the result can be just as painful. Stendhal compared it to “a pistol shot in the middle of a concert, something loud and vulgar, and yet a thing to which it is not possible to refuse one’s attention.” Sometimes, a political agenda is slathered on top of an otherwise unrelated story like a coat of high-gloss paint. Or else characters are manipulated like ventriloquist dummies to dramatize a writer’s views, usually at the expense of their credibility. The critic Becca Rothfeld coined the term sanctimony literature to describe a wave of popular contemporary novels whose protagonists are represented as good people because they espouse the right progressive views in between couplings and breakups. The politics is already settled, with no conflicts in the quest for goodness, only a smooth convergence of opinion among authors, characters, and readers: frictionless fiction. If the book world were predominantly conservative, sanctimony literature would present very different views. But that’s almost inconceivable. We’ve had groups called “Hispanics for Trump,” “Blacks for Trump,” and even “Arab Americans for Trump,” but I have serious trouble imagining “Poets, Essayists, and Novelists for Trump.” It’s even hard to think of a living American writer who could be a registered Republican—Cormac McCarthy might have been the last. It’s a sign of the saturation of culture by politics that the book world is so uniformly on the left. Perhaps there’s a progressive bias to literature itself: an openness to new varieties of experience, an impulse to criticize the existing social order. Yet other times and places had their conservative and reactionary writers—critics of liberal democracy, skeptics of progress and equality: Dostoyevsky, Conrad, Eliot, Pound, Céline, Hurston, O’Connor. Maybe we should congratulate ourselves on having no prize-winning fascist poets. But in the 1940s, another period when literature came under the domination of politics, Trilling warned: “We have the books that point out the bad conditions, that praise us for taking progressive attitudes. We have no books that raise questions in our minds not only about conditions but about ourselves, that lead us to refine our motives and ask what might lie behind our good impulses.” When literature applies no pressure to a general conformity, we read to be flattered and lose a crucial tool in understanding reality, including the murky nature of our deepest beliefs. Literary judgments merge with political ones until they’re indistinguishable. It ought to be possible to say: “This writer speaks for me—too bad he’s a terrible writer.” But readers, including professional critics, are more likely to assess the merits of a book before they’ve opened it. A judge for a prestigious prize once told me with evident pride that his committee had decided not to honor the book they thought was actually the best, but the one they thought was most politically relevant to the moment. Some literary prizes are so aligned with current orthodoxy that every few years, the winners reliably change with the political fashions. I think this confusion of categories shows a waning faith in both politics and literature. Politics becomes a set of positions and slogans, not a public square where individuals encounter one another in a common enterprise, ideas and interests clash, and no one comes out completely clean. Literature becomes a demonstration of goodness, not the art form in which our humanity can be most fully explored. The point is not to keep literature and politics separate. That would be not just impossible but undesirable—in fact, unthinkable. We would lose, among so much more, the Philip Roth of The Plot Against America. Politics is the business of everyone, including writers. Their work can be done only in an artistic freedom that needs political freedom to flourish. They have to balance the inner solitude of art with a nourishing connection to the outside world. Nothing about their vocation equips them any better than other people to answer the hardest questions confronting humanity—but neither are writers excused from the responsibility to face them. “A writer should not provide solutions,” Chekhov said, “but describe a situation so truthfully that the reader can no longer evade it.” Sensitive readers know when the authorial thumb is on the scale—when they’re being recruited and flattered rather than enlightened and provoked. Filling in what Gessen calls “the many shades and colors of the grid” should be the aspiration of any literature worth the name. If Roth had written American Pastoral to lay down some basic moral coordinates, this tale of a decent, successful Jewish businessman whose precocious daughter becomes a 1960s revolutionary and blows up their lives would pander to the complacency of a conservative Jewish reader. In fact, Norman Podhoretz loved it, while missing the point. Roth’s masterpiece expresses all his ambivalence about assimilation and rebellion; in the end, there are no ideological winners, only the “massive historical pain” that the “indigenous American berserk” inflicts on the novel’s uncomprehending hero. The novelist’s job is to bring abstract ideology into sustained contact with concrete experience. There, a mysterious transformation takes place; ideas never keep their pristine shape as they undergo the heat of human passions. Writers and readers are brought into a communion that’s higher than political opinion and, as Irving Howe wrote in his classic Politics and the Novel , “find some common recognition, some supervening human bond above and beyond ideas.” W hy should all of this matter to us now? The world’s richest and most powerful men want to hustle us into a post-human age of history. They anticipate that our ability in relation to superintelligence will be about the same as that of chimpanzees is to us. Elon Musk recently predicted that in five years, “There really won’t be anything that AI can’t do better than humans, apart from being human perhaps.” The dismissive shrug of that perhaps ! Musk makes being human sound like an afterthought, hardly worth mentioning. In the future, and soon, there will be something shameful and humiliating about it, stuck as we’ll be with our decaying bodies and primitive brains, struggling to put a few good sentences together, while machines fed with every human word ever written spit out perfect novels in a matter of seconds. We’ll have returned to the opening scene of 2001: A Space Odyssey , where shaggy hominids chatter moronically at the base of an inscrutable monolith. [ From the April 1969 issue: The journey of Philip Roth ] I haven’t read an AI novel and hope I never will, though it might happen without my knowing. After all, artificial novels have won major literary prizes, before researchers discovered the fraud through the detector Pangram, which is becoming a kind of literary Patriot-missile system, our only defense against the onslaught of machine literature. It’s also possible that 100 percent human-written texts will start to sound more like generative AI. Large language models are trained on our work, but the flow of instruction could be reversed, the way that algorithms dictate how we sound on social-media platforms where we think we’re free to sound like ourselves. The more that our writing is done through AI, the more reductive and predictable and cloying it will become, like a robot lover in book form. It might not spell the end of literature, but it will probably mean the end of the kind of literature we’ve known throughout the democratic centuries—the work of a free individual mind. And if writing serves as the valet to a domineering politics that decides which ideas and writers are allowed into the house of literature—if writers lose faith in the principle that makes their work possible just when it stands to be swept aside by a trillion-dollar industry—then the whole thing might as well be done by machine, and probably will be. With the right prompts, AI will surely excel at laying down basic moral coordinates. But if the creation of stories and the communication of ideas through language remain activities that differentiate us from computers and chimps, then literature will be one of the last barriers against surrendering our humanity to the million-headed god of superintelligence. If books written by human beings are to survive the hyper-politicization of this age and the artificiality of the next, it will be because this work does something special, something we want and need and can’t get anywhere else. On the verge of the singularity, we must cherish our words and the freedom to write them as flickers of that absurd and precious thing: human dignity.

items.title: Mise en garde des personnes âgées contre les infections respiratoires
items.description: Dr Afef Hammami, spécialiste en gériatrie, a recommandé aux personnes âgées de se faire vacciner contre la grippe saisonnière et de prendre les précautions nécessaires dans leur mode de vie quotidien à l’approche de l’hiver, afin d’éviter les infections respiratoires, eu égard le vieillissement de leur système immunitaire et la diminution de sa capacité à réagir rapidement et efficacement face à ces maladies. Dans une déclaration à l’agence Tap, ce dimanche 8 novembre 2026, Dr Hammami a expliqué que la réponse du système immunitaire face aux maladies s’affaiblit à partir de l’âge de 60 ans, bien que ce phénomène varie d’une personne âgée à l’autre. Ce déclin est plus marqué chez les individus souffrant de maladies chroniques ou chez ceux qui consomment des antibiotiques de manière inappropriée, a-t-elle ajouté. Le froid ne provoque pas nécessairement des infections respiratoires, mais il convient d’adopter un mode de vie sain pour limiter ces risques, a souligné Drr Hammami. Cela inclut notamment l’aération régulière des pièces, l’éloignement des enfants malades des personnes âgées, l’arrêt du tabac, une hydratation suffisante, la pratique d’une activité physique adaptée, ainsi que le renforcement du système immunitaire grâce à une alimentation saine, telle que le régime méditerranéen. Par ailleurs, Dr Hammami a recommandé de se rendre sans tarder au service des urgences le plus proche dès l’apparition de symptômes évocateurs d’une infection respiratoire, en précisant que ces signes peuvent varier entre les personnes âgées et les enfants ; chez les seniors, ils peuvent se manifester par une absence de fièvre, une altération de l’état de conscience, une grande faiblesse, une fatigue intense, une baisse du taux d’oxygène dans le sang ou encore des douleurs thoraciques. La praticienne fait référence à une étude médicale tunisienne, publiée en 2026 dans une revue scientifique reconnue et portant sur les maladies respiratoires chez un échantillon de 2 038 patients ayant consulté les services d’urgence de 11 hôpitaux publics et 85 cliniques privées. L’étude a conclu que 31,6 % de ces patients sont des personnes âgées de plus de 65 ans, et que seuls 4,9 % des personnes composant cet échantillon avaient été vaccinées contre la grippe saisonnière. I. B. L’article Mise en garde des personnes âgées contre les infections respiratoires est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: ‘Special connection with Pakistan’: US Senator Van Hollen, eyeing 2028 presidential bid, was born in Karachi
items.description: US Democrat Senator Christopher Van Hollen, who has set his sights on the 2028 contest for the American presidential office, was born in Karachi. According to his biography on Maryland Manual Online — a website run by the Maryland state government — he was born in the port city in 1959. Van Hollen himself spoke of his “special connection” with Pakistan in a clip released on the country’s Independence Day last year. “I am proud to join you in celebrating Pakistan’s 79th Independence Day. I am fortunate to have a special connection with Pakistan, having been born in Karachi as the son of an American foreign service officer. “Throughout my life, I have experienced first-hand the generosity, the goodness and the determination of the Pakistani people. I am proud to celebrate the strong people-to-people ties between our two countries […] I look forward to further strengthening the ties of friendship between the Americans and the Pakistani people,” he said in a short message. In 2021, Van Hollen had thanked Pakistan among other countries for helping evacuate American nationals and others stranded in Afghanistan following the Taliban takeover of the country. In the aftermath of the devastating 2022 floods , he met with then-foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari to discuss how the US can continue to assist efforts to help flood-affected people. In February 2024, he wrote to Pakistan’s then-envoy, Ambassador Masood Khan, urging Pakistani authorities to fully investigate the allegations of fraud and electoral interference in the Feb 8 general elections. He stressed that respecting the people’s mandate was the “only way a new government will be empowered to tackle issues facing Pakistan such as negotiating a new IMF agreement or investing to mitigate future floods”. Apart from Pakistan, the Maryland senator also spent time in India, where he studied at Kodaikanal International School in the Tamil Nadu state. He later studied philosophy at Swarthmore College, followed by his Master’s in public policy from Harvard University. He earned his Juris Doctor degree from Georgetown University and was admitted to Maryland Bar in 1990. He has been a member of the US Senate since January 2017. Previously, he had also been a member of the US House of Representatives from 2003 to 2017. Following the Republicans’ thumping defeat in the recently held midterms, Van Hollen was seen as the potential candidate for the Senate majority leader. However, he put the speculation to rest by telling Fox 5 , which is owned by the Fox Broadcasting Company, that he had “made clear that I’m not looking to be the next Democratic leader. I’ve been kicking the tyres on a 2028 presidential election“.

items.title: Le Sénégal, ce géant aux imperfections magnifiques (par Moussa DIOP)
items.description: Depuis une semaine, chaque fois que j’ai le cafard, et les occasions ne manquent pas, je m’offre un nouveau shoot d’un extrait de cette désormais mythique cérémonie d’ouverture des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse Dakar 2026. Il en ressort une conviction : l’Afrique est un géant, le Sénégal n’est pas petit. Un terroir de cœur pour un continent de 54 pays. Le Sénégal est un pays exceptionnel. Mais l’exception n’est pas toujours synonyme de perfection. Dans cette cérémonie tant vantée, il y a eu des couacs… Oui, oui !Dans cette majestueuse fresque où l’Afrique s’est dessinée point par point, portée par l’humanité et incarnée par des présences humaines, quelques imperfections de rondeurs se sont glissées. Les deux chiffres « 2 » de 2026 n’étaient pas tout à fait parfaits. La représentation de Dakar comportait, elle aussi, quelques approximations. Mais peu importe. L’essentiel était ailleurs : montrer l’Afrique telle qu’elle est, dans sa réalité et sa complexité, et non telle qu’on la fantasme trop souvent. Oui, le Sénégal est un pays exceptionnellement imparfait. Sur le chemin du stade Abdoulaye Wade, devenu, en ce 31 octobre 2026, un lieu de mémoire, une phrase est restée en écho : « Vos sourires serviront de lumière dans la soirée. » Il est 17 h 35. Un membre du personnel, parmi les volontaires, s’empare de son mégaphone et lance cette phrase avec une douceur qui lui donne des allures de vérité. Bien après cette soirée émerveillée, ces mots continueront de résonner dans les profondeurs de la mémoire collective africaine. Oui, le volontaire avait raison. Il y a eu un véritable hymne à la joie, porté par des Sénégalais et des Africains ébahis. Ce soir-là, le spectacle proposé a fait naître des sourires, véritables lumières dans la nuit profonde. Le code épique, le code mythique et le code mythologique s’entrelacent pour mieux entrer en symbiose. La voix de Kiné Lam prend une dimension singulière sur un sample de « Niani Niani Bañ na », œuvre pluridécennale de Samba Kumba Kalado Dioum. Elle retrace l’épopée du refus face à un destin que l’on voudrait inéluctable : de l’annonce faite à Lat Dior au refus de Niani Kalankadougou de se soumettre sans combattre. Dans l’un des couplets, Kiné Lam revient sur un épisode et une valeur essentiels : « Samba Bineta Mame Jéej Joor ñu bañ koo yóbbu déeg bu delloo nguur ga… » Cette capacité à refuser l’indignité, à ferrailler pour l’honneur, à tenir tête aux puissants pour protéger les faibles. La cérémonie de ce samedi historique a fait rejaillir le feu d’un ancien volcan que l’on croyait trop vieux. Et ces sentiments ne quittent pas ce peuple, héritier de valeurs, de vertus et d’une histoire culturelle si riche et si enviée. Ce substrat n’est pas une simple écume des choses. Il n’est pas non plus un écueil sur le chemin de l’excellence. Il constitue, au contraire, l’une des forces profondes qui ont permis au Sénégal de s’illustrer bien au-delà de ses frontières, en plaçant plusieurs de ses fils à la tête de grandes institutions internationales, comme l’Unesco (Amadou Mahtar Mbow), la Fao (Jacques Diouf) et l’Iaaf (Lamine Diack), ou encore en leur permettant de rayonner sur l’échiquier économique international, à l’image de Makhtar Diop (Ifc), de Moussa Touré, de Hadjibou Soumaré et d’Abdoulaye Diop, qui ont tous occupé la présidence de la Commission de l’Uemoa. Notre terroir a également connu trois alternances politiques pacifiques (2000, 2012 et 2024), cultivé une diversité religieuse et culturelle remarquable et préservé la parenté à plaisanterie qui, dans les périodes troubles de l’esclavage, servait de bouclier et permettait de masquer certaines de nos failles intimes. Ainsi, l’existence de paradoxes est aussi visible qu’un diadème sur un front : un potentiel économique encore insuffisamment exploité, le chômage des jeunes, les inégalités, les difficultés du système éducatif, les défis de gouvernance et les tensions sociales. Certes. Mais le Sénégal demeure, prosaïquement, le seul pays de moins de 20 millions d’habitants à avoir remporté la Coupe d’Afrique des nations de football à deux reprises. Si Alkebulan, le continent-mère, berceau de l’humanité, l’Afrique, enfanta le monde, le Sénégal en est peut-être le fils aîné. moussa.diop@lesoleil.sn

items.title: Sénégal : au moins 21 morts dans le naufrage d'une pirogue de migrants
items.description: Au moins vingt-et-une personnes sont mortes dans le naufrage d'une pirogue de migrants au large de Kébémer, dans le nord-ouest du Sénégal où, selon les autorités, les recherches d'éventuels survivants se poursuivent. Des milliers de personnes originaires d'Afrique de l'Ouest, en majorité des jeunes, tentent depuis des années de gagner clandestinement l'Europe en empruntant la route de l'Atlantique, principalement vers l'archipel espagnol des Canaries, à bord d’embarcations surchargées, souvent vétustes. « Au soir du 7 novembre 2026, le bilan provisoire fait état de 21 corps sans vie et d'un rescapé », a indiqué le ministère sénégalais de l'Intérieur dans un communiqué, qui ne précise pas le jour du drame. « Les services compétents de l'État sont mobilisés pour poursuivre les recherches, porter secours aux éventuels rescapés et accompagner les familles », a-t-il ajouté. Le ministre de l'Intérieur est attendu sur le site du drame lundi. Selon le quotidien national Le Soleil, le naufrage est produit au large des côtes de la localité de Loumpoul, dans la région de Louga (département de Kébémer), entre Dakar et Saint-Louis. « La plupart des victimes seraient originaires des communes de Léona et de Thiéppe », dans le même département, ajoute le quotidien. Les passeurs dans le collimateur Samedi également, la gendarmerie sénégalaise a annoncé avoir intercepté au large de Dakar 142 migrants clandestins, dont des femmes et des enfants, qui tentaient de rejoindre l'Espagne à bord d'une pirogue. L'opération a eu lieu vendredi et a été menée « en marge de la couverture sécuritaire » des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) de Dakar, le tout premier événement olympique à se dérouler sur le sol africain. Parmi les personnes interceptées figurent 40 Sénégalais dont quatre femmes, 93 Gambiens dont 17 femmes, un ressortissant de Guinée-Bissau, deux Guinéens et deux Nigérians, selon la gendarmerie. Le groupe comptait également deux nourrissons et deux enfants mineurs, ajoute-t-elle. The post Sénégal : au moins 21 morts dans le naufrage d'une pirogue de migrants appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Pakistan-built robots serve taste of future to Karachi diners
items.description: Wheeling its way between dining booths at a neon-lit restaurant in Karachi, a robot waitress drops off a fresh pizza to an awaiting family. While global buzz is growing around agile humanoids made in the United States, China and elsewhere, robotic staff are a rare sight in the South Asian country. “Welcome to Sicilian. My name is Robia,” the waitress says in an electronic voice, looking down at diners through blinking red LED eyes. This photograph taken on October 2, 2026 shows Robia (R) and Jojo (2R), humanoid robot waitresses serving customers at The Sicilian restaurant in Karachi. — AFP Robia and her colleague Jojo are the DIY creations of Pakistani engineer Syed Osama Aziz, who is bringing a sci-fi reboot to Karachi’s storied dining scene. They have spherical white heads and dark visors, similar to a motorcycle helmet, and sport black shawls around their neck in the style of a dupatta . Aziz, who also established The Sicilian restaurant, developed the machines using mostly locally manufactured parts, designing their circuit boards and programming them in his own lab. “The equipment, the things needed to make robots, are not so easily available here, so we had to arrange them,” he told AFP . This photograph taken on September 30, 2026 shows a robotics software engineer Syed Osama Aziz working on robot components at his workshop in Multan. — AFP The duo were developed through his robotics company, Cobot, with help from friends and some electronic components imported from abroad. In China and other East Asian countries especially, robots are an increasingly common sight , shuttling food to customers in chain restaurants and taking on other jobs from cleaning to greeting hotel guests. But they remain a novelty in Pakistan, where Aziz’s home-grown creations are attracting curious diners. When they arrive at a table, the customers must either take the food off their serving tray themselves or wait for a human member of staff to assist them. This photograph taken on October 2, 2026 shows a staff passing food orders to Robia, a humanoid robot waitress at The Sicilian restaurant in Karachi. — AFP Excited customers Aziz, whose workshop manufacturing the robots is located in Multan, hopes to make his creations more sophisticated in the future. “Our plans are to add camera-based processing and image-processing features,” he said. “That means the robot will also recognise you by looking at you, and it will remember what you ordered last time, and accordingly it will be able to give you better suggestions.” For now, the robots are proving a hit with families, who flock to the restaurant to watch the machines in action. This photograph taken on October 2, 2026 shows children playing around Robia, a humanoid robot waitress at The Sicilian restaurant in Karachi. — AFP “The best thing about it is that it introduces itself,” excited customer Ahmer Zameer told AFP , explaining the robot also “tells you what things you can order”. Children reach out to touch the robots while their parents snap photographs and selfies. Young customer Sonia Dilosker said she was impressed by the androids’ appearance and preferred their approach to serving customers, “because it is a machine and without any emotions”. Restaurant staff say the novelty has brought a surge in customers — some travelling from across the sprawling port city to meet the robots. This photograph taken on October 2, 2026 shows Robia, a humanoid robot waitress serving customers at The Sicilian restaurant in Karachi. — AFP “Our business has grown. People are coming from far away for this. They have seen a robot for the first time here,” staff member Hellen told AFP . “People are excited to see this.” Header image: This photograph taken on October 2, 2026 shows Robia, a humanoid robot waitress serving customers at The Sicilian restaurant in Karachi. — AFP

items.title: Tempted by snacks before bed? Here’s why – and what you can do about it
items.description: You’ve eaten dinner, you’re comfortably full, and yet half an hour later you’re raiding the kitchen cupboards. Sound familiar? Research suggests that about a third of people are snacking every night after their evening meal – for those aged 18-24, four in five are unable to resist. Dietitian Dr Kristine Beaulieu says this spells trouble. She points to evidence showing that the more people eat within two hours of going to bed, the “greater the odds” of weight gain and obesity. So, why are evening cravings so common? And what can you do to keep them in check? Appetite peaks in the evening Despite the fact we spend longer going without food when we are sleeping, research suggests our appetite naturally peaks in the evening, almost regardless of how much we have eaten earlier in the day. Prof James Betts, who researches how the body handles food and energy at the University of Bath, says a big factor is that our “hunger hormone” ghrelin is generally higher later in the day. “While it tends to be suppressed by meals, that really only happens after the first meal of the day, not after lunch or dinner.” But what you eat also matters. Meals rich in protein, fibre and volume tend to keep us satisfied for longer. Betts says not having a nutritious or satiating evening meal can lead to a “crash” later, which sees people snack. For others, the fear of waking up hungry during the night is also a motivating factor, while habit plays a role too. “If snacking often happens in the same setting, the surrounding cues can start to trigger cravings,” says Prof Suzanne Higgs, an expert in appetite at the University of Birmingham. “For example, if someone usually snacks while watching TV, simply turning the TV on may make them feel like eating.” Why sweet treats are so tempting It’s not just feelings of hunger that increase later in the day. Research suggests our appetite for calorie-dense foods also becomes stronger, driven by the brain’s reward system rather than a genuine need for energy. “Our liking and wanting for high-fat foods are greater later in the day compared to low-fat foods,” says Beaulieu, who splits her time between the University of Leeds and University of Moncton in Canada. “That hedonic drive can override signals of fullness, making us want to snack or eat a dessert even though we’re full.” Even after a substantial evening meal, foods rich in sugar, fat or salt can continue to activate reward pathways in the brain, helping explain why many people find themselves reaching for something more. So when you find yourself standing in front of the biscuit tin at 9pm, it may not be a lack of willpower. Your biology is stacked against you. Does snacking make it harder to sleep? The evidence is mixed. But certainly eating a large meal late affects digestion and the body’s normal preparation for sleep. What about snacking? Here the research becomes less clear. There is some evidence that foods high in refined carbohydrates and added sugars, from white bread and white rice to biscuits and cakes, may be linked to poorer sleep. Researchers think this could be because such foods cause bigger swings in blood sugar levels and may alter some of the hormonal signals involved in regulating sleep and appetite. However, teasing out cause and effect is difficult. People with poor sleep may be more likely to snack on sugary foods. “Sleep deprivation is known to not only increase appetite, but also a desire for energy-dense foods,” says Prof Jonathan Johnston, a sleep and body clock expert at the University of Surrey. It means it is very difficult to draw firm conclusions on whether snacking in late evening disrupts sleep, says Betts. “The evidence is far from clear and perhaps may reflect that some people respond differently to others to different foods before bed.” How to snack in a healthier way First, work out what’s driving the snacking. If you are genuinely hungry, it may help to make earlier meals more filling If snacking is mainly habitual, changing routines and planning snacks in advance can help “Eating while distracted, for instance watching TV, can lead people to consume more because they pay less attention to how much they’ve eaten,” says Higgs. But there’s no need to ban evening snacks completely, says Beaulieu. A reasonable portion of something enjoyable is often more sustainable Keep healthy options, such as fruit, yoghurt and nuts available Even a little chocolate every now and then is not the end of the world “It’s OK to eat those craved foods once in a while in moderation.” The trick, she says, is to make the healthy choice the default. “If those craved foods aren’t in the cupboard on a regular basis and a healthy option is, it means you are more likely to choose the healthier option.”

items.title: RETHINKING PAKISTAN’S AUTO POLICY
items.description: For one woman interviewed for the 2019 social assessment of Karachi’s planned Yellow Line Bus Rapid Transit (BRT), getting to her job destination meant walking 20 minutes to a road crossing, paying for a rickshaw and then paying again for a bus. Other women interviewed for the assessment relied on shared three-wheelers that waited to fill up with passengers before leaving. For some, the journey could take two hours each way. Monthly transport costs ranged from Rs3,000 to Rs6,000 in households where incomes of Rs20,000 to Rs30,000 were common. Fares can eat into an already modest wage. An unreliable connection can make a worker late. A second fare at each end of the journey can make studying at a college or a job across town too expensive a proposition to take up. The draft for Pakistan’s Auto Policy 2026-31 revolves around car prices, manufacturers and tariffs. Yet, most households in the country own no car and struggle with the daily cost of commuting. Mobility for work, education and healthcare remains restricted due to unavailability of affordable and safe public transportation choices. How can Pakistan’s auto policy serve the people at large and not just the top decile of households in the country? THE FAULT IN OUR DRAFTS In April, when petrol rose by more than Rs137 a litre, governments briefly treated the price of a bus ticket as a cost-of-living issue. Islamabad announced 30 days of free public transport. Punjab’s relief ran for 69 days, with authorities estimating that hundreds of thousands of passengers a day used the free services. The relief ended, but the daily cost of getting to work remained. Pakistan now has a chance to address some of that cost through its next auto policy. The draft Auto Policy 2026-31 has been okayed by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif but is still awaiting final approval as the Ministry of Industries and Production is set to forward the draft policy to the Ministry of Finance, which aims to share it with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for review. This policy would reportedly reduce tariffs, open a formal route for commercial used-car imports and expand the role of electric vehicles. These changes could give car buyers more choice. The draft also shapes how buses and two-wheelers are taxed, which vehicles get incentives and where the proceeds of a proposed automobile levy go. The problem, in my view, is that the debate remains organised around the vehicle and its producer. The household experiences it as a sequence of fares, waits and transfers. An auto policy cannot run provincial bus services, but it can reduce fleet costs and make public support conditional on affordable service. That connects industrial policy to the ability to earn a living. Those decisions should be judged by what they do for the journeys people make every day. For most Pakistani households, the price of a bus ride is a more immediate concern than the price of a new car. WHO’S BUYING THE ALTO? Pakistan’s assemblers sold 155,631 passenger cars in 2025-26. Including separately reported jeeps and pick-ups takes four-wheeler sales to about 206,000. Motorcycle and rickshaw sales totalled roughly 1.97 million. My analysis of the 2024-25 Household Integrated Economic Survey (HIES) shows how differently Pakistanis get around. About 6.6 percent of households own a car and 57 percent own a motorcycle. Roughly 41 percent own neither. Among the poorest fifth of urban households, nearly two-thirds have neither vehicle and only about one in a thousand own a car. Among the richest urban fifth, more than one in five own a car. A Suzuki Alto VXR lists at about Rs2.99 million. The survey puts average household income at Rs82,179 a month, so the Alto costs more than three years of total income, before a household pays for food, rent or anything else. One reported estimate puts the likely reduction in small-car prices under the Auto Policy draft at around nine percent over five years. Applied to the Alto, that would still leave it costing about 33 months of average household income. There is a case for bringing those prices down faster. In 2006-07, local assemblers sold 180,834 cars, whereas passenger car sales reached just 155,631 in 2025-26. The figures are imperfectly comparable because classifications have changed and SUVs have become a bigger part of the market. Still, Indus Motors estimates that the industry can assemble about 600,000 vehicles a year and uses roughly 30 percent of that capacity. New manufacturers have entered the market, but factories still have far more capacity than the market can absorb. The entry of more assemblers does not by itself resolve this. If each operates a small plant behind similar tariff protection, the market can acquire more brands without acquiring the scale or price competition consumers need. Lower duties on finished cars would strengthen the pressure to compete, but duties on imported components also matter. A sensible transition should expose producers to competition while allowing them to obtain inputs at competitive prices. For some smaller imported cars, one reported tariff schedule keeps customs duty at 50 percent for the first two years and then brings it down in stages to 15 percent by 2030-31. Bringing those cuts forward would put earlier pressure on local producers to compete on price and quality. If the government also wants to discourage fuel-hungry vehicles, it can tax size or fuel use directly. A cut in customs duty does not translate directly into an equal cut in the showroom price. Exchange rates, other taxes and producer margins impact what the buyer pays. I would judge success by actual prices and product quality, rather than the number of assembly licences issued. A tariff timetable that can repeatedly be deferred offers consumers little assurance. Although Pakistan’s local car manufacturing capacity has more than doubled since 2006, annual sales (as denoted by the blue line) across the years have remained at a stagnated level | Author’s analysis of data sourced from the PIDE and the Pakistan Automotive Manufacturers Association (Pama) AN ELECTRIC SOLUTION? The distribution of electric vehicle incentives deserves the same scrutiny. Some reported proposals for electric cars include a favourable sales tax rate and a financing ceiling of Rs10 million. If a 17 percentage-point tax preference (the difference between tax rates on electric vehicles as compared to on an internal combustion engine vehicle) is applied to an Rs8 million pre-tax car, the buyer’s tax advantage would be Rs1.36 million. That is roughly the value of 21 electric-motorcycle subsidies of Rs65,000 each under the Pakistan Accelerated Vehicle Electrification (PAVE) programme. The actual benefit would depend on how the tax is applied and what the government ultimately approves. The comparison shows how much support can go to a single purchase. Equivalent fiscal support does not mean equal benefits from different vehicles. A higher loan ceiling does little for someone without a down payment or an income that a lender will accept. Eligibility matters as much as the advertised concession. Electric cars can cut petrol use, especially for people who drive long distances. But a household that cannot finance any private vehicle needs a different kind of help. A bus fare can determine whether someone in that household works at all. Car ownership remains heavily concentrated among wealthier households, while most urban Pakistanis in the lower income brackets have no personal vehicle | Author’s analysis of HIES 2024-25 data THE HIDDEN COST OF BEING UNABLE TO TRAVEL The poorest fifth of Pakistani households spent 4.8 percent of their budgets on transport, compared with 6.7 percent for the richest fifth. In cities, the respective figures are 4.2 and 6.5 percent. If spending were the measure of need, the figures would suggest transport was a bigger problem for the rich. But consider: a household survey counts the fare someone paid. It has no fare to record when a worker walks to save money, a woman turns down a job she cannot reach safely or a student stays home because college is too far away. The poorest fifth also spends almost half its budget on food, compared with about 29 percent for the richest fifth. Once food and the estimated rental value of housing are set aside, transport takes up a more similar share of what remains. The estimated rent includes the value of living in an owner-occupied home, even though no rent changes hands. Removing it from the comparison does not create cash for a bus ticket — it changes the denominator. I read the low transport share as a reason to investigate journeys people cannot make. The expenditure survey alone cannot tell us how many jobs were declined or classes missed. My analysis puts transport spending for the poorest fifth at about Rs254 per person a month. At Rs20 a ride, that pays for six complete return trips. A World Bank benchmark used in urban transport affordability studies allows for roughly 60 one-way trips a month. Even if someone in the poorest fifth put their entire transport budget towards a bus, they would still be well short of a month’s travel to work or school. Among poor urban households with at least one earner and neither a car nor a motorcycle, the survey implies about Rs9 in reported in-city fares per earner per working day. People may forget small fares when asked to recall spending over a year. The figures also cannot separate journeys made on foot from those abandoned altogether. Project documents for Karachi’s Red Line BRT estimate that about 40 percent of trips in the city are made on foot or by bicycle. Some people choose to walk or cycle. For others, it may be the only way to avoid paying for several rides on a single journey. The cost is easier to see against a wage. My analysis of the survey puts median monthly earnings for an urban paid worker at about Rs32,000. At Rs80 each way over 26 working days, the commute costs Rs4,160, or 13 percent of pay. A combination of wagons and rickshaws costing Rs200 a day takes Rs5,200, or more than 16 percent of pay. At the household level, two earners, each paying Rs20 in both directions over 26 working days, would spend Rs2,080 a month. Against the roughly Rs40,146 monthly budget for the poorest urban households in my analysis, that is just over five percent. At Rs80, the same journeys cost Rs8,320, or about 21 percent. These comparisons use survey-period budgets and illustrative fares, not today’s measured burden. They show why a fare that looks modest per trip can be unaffordable when paid repeatedly. For women in paid urban work, reported median monthly earnings were about Rs10,000, partly reflecting fewer hours of paid work. A 26-day commute at Rs80 each way would take about 42 percent of that amount. This is an illustration, since a woman earning Rs10,000 may work fewer days. It shows what fares can do to the gains from taking on more work. Distance can also put education out of reach. In the survey, about 1.3 million girls and young women and 900,000 boys and young men aged five to 24 had never attended school and cited distance as the reason. Where there is a school to go to, a safe, affordable journey can remove one of the barriers to getting there. Motorcycle ownership only partly solves this problem. A single motorcycle cannot necessarily serve two earners travelling in different directions and children going to school. Nor can we assume that every household member can ride it. Therefore, counting households with a vehicle tells us less than knowing who can use it, when and for which journeys. The economics of commuting favours public transport, as demonstrated by this comparison across one month | Author’s analysis of data sourced from the World Bank, PIDE and HIES A BUS PEOPLE CAN RELY ON On Lahore’s Orange Line train, about 51 percent of reported journeys were for work and 33 percent for education. In Peshawar, a 2023 account citing TransPeshawar (a public company established by the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to manage, operate and maintain the Zu Peshawar BRT system) put women at about 30 percent of passengers on the bus rapid transit system, up from an estimated two percent on earlier services. Other published accounts put the newer figure closer to 20 percent. The new system offered separate entrances and reserved areas, better lighting, station security and more predictable service. Research in Lahore by economists Robert Garlick, Erica Field and Kate Vyborny offers a closer look at how transport impacts decisions about work. Through a job-search platform, the researchers offered commuting services to women. The offer of women-only transport more than doubled job application rates, while mixed-gender transport produced little response. The study measured applications, not jobs secured. It shows how the commute can deter women before an employer has even seen their names. Even a new bus can be difficult to board. Writing in Eos earlier this year, Samina Hassan Laghari and Arif Hasan described Karachi’s electric buses with about 30 seats carrying 70 or 80 people, sometimes more than 100. Women told them they had given up work because of the journey. The city’s bus fleet was reported at 1,029, against an estimated requirement of 15,000. Building more corridors can help, but people have to reach them. A cheap fare on the main route can lose much of its value if a passenger has to pay for a rickshaw to get to it. A well-lit stop is of limited use to a child who has to cross a dangerous road to reach it. The World Health Organisation (WHO) estimates roughly 28,000 road deaths a year in Pakistan, with pedestrians accounting for a large share. Official reported totals are much lower. Both the walk to the bus and the ride itself belong in a transport plan. Reliability matters as much as the fare. A daily-wage worker who cannot tell whether a bus will arrive in five minutes or 45 has to leave early or risk losing a shift. Karachi’s Red Line has faced a much longer timetable than originally envisaged. While cities build major corridors, they also need buses running between neighbourhoods, regular departures and connections that people can use without building an hour’s uncertainty into the day. A dependable service also reduces the unpaid time a worker must allow for delays. Time savings belong in the economic appraisal, even when they produce no additional fare revenue. They should be measured through actual waiting and journey times, rather than assumed whenever a new bus or corridor is announced. THE COST OF THE COMMUTE To compare the choices, I modelled the same trip across five modes, with 30 kilometres covered a day, 26 days a month. For private vehicles, the calculation includes ownership and financing costs as well as fuel or electricity. For the bus passenger, it includes a low main fare and some travel to and from the route. Under these assumptions, monthly costs per commuter are roughly Rs1,900 for a bus, Rs4,900 for an electric motorcycle, Rs5,200 for wagons and rickshaws, Rs7,000 for a petrol motorcycle and Rs39,900 for a small petrol car. The bus estimate includes a Rs25 fare and feeder journeys. The model assumes petrol at Rs378 a litre, 15 percent vehicle financing and some sharing of private vehicles. These are modelled costs, not quoted monthly instalments. The bus figure is what the passenger pays after public support; it is not the full cost of providing the service. The difference matters for the country’s import bill as well as the commuter’s wallet. Pakistan spent about $16.9 billion on petroleum imports in fiscal year (FY)26, compared with roughly $2.1 billion on imported vehicle assembly kits. The totals cover different categories, but they give a sense of the scale of dependence on imported fuel. In the model, moving one million daily commuters from motorcycles into small petrol cars would add about Rs394 billion a year to household costs and roughly $440 million to imports, including fuel and vehicles. Electric motorcycles offer substantial savings where people already ride petrol bikes. In the model, each rupee of public support for electric motorcycles saves households more cash and generally saves more on imports than a rupee spent on buses. A bus reaches people a motorcycle subsidy cannot readily serve, including students, older passengers and households that cannot buy a vehicle. That makes a case for supporting both. The journey being replaced matters. A bus carrying former wagon passengers has a different effect on imports from one attracting motorists. An electric motorcycle replacing a petrol motorcycle is different from an additional vehicle bought for convenience. My calculations assume those substitutions — they are not a forecast that every subsidised purchase will deliver the same saving. I would assess the programmes against what riders actually stop using. There is a case for electric buses on routes where charging and electricity supply can support them. In an illustrative comparison, a diesel bus covering 80,000 kilometres a year uses about 18,000 litres of fuel. At the diesel price of Rs395.20 a litre, effective on November 3, that costs about Rs7.1 million. Meanwhile, an electric bus, using about 96,000 units of power at an assumed Rs39.70 per unit, would spend about Rs3.8 million on electricity. The roughly Rs3.3 million difference comes before maintenance, financing and battery costs. A city weighing the higher purchase price should count that annual saving and the reduced exposure to a diesel price spike. Battery replacements and charging equipment also belong in the calculation. High utilisation helps recover the higher purchase price only if charging arrangements allow buses to run the promised service. Electric buses eliminate exhaust at the roadside, but overall emissions also depend on electricity generation. A national pollution claim needs a separate estimate. Women and men pictured driving electric bikes in Lahore: electric motorcycles offer substantial savings where people already ride petrol bikes | White Star HOW MANY BUSES CAN A LEVY BUY? The Automotive Development Levy (ADL), proposed in the draft for the Auto Policy 2026-31, could raise around Rs232 billion over five years. Its reported uses include export rebates and industrial upgrading. The government should consider putting a share towards public transport and say which proposed uses it would scale back to do so. Spread evenly, the projected revenue comes to about Rs46 billion a year. In my model, an electric bus running around 70,000 kilometres a year with 800 passenger boardings a day needs about Rs21.5 million in annual public support if borrowing costs 18 percent. At 11 percent, the contribution falls by about Rs5.5 million, to roughly Rs16 million. At that lower cost, the entire annual levy could support close to 2,900 buses. Using only a share would pay for proportionately fewer. The levy still needs approval and the figures depend on what buses cost, how much operators collect in fares and how many people ride. The assumptions also deserve scrutiny before anyone commits public money. Eight hundred boardings are not 800 different people: a commuter travelling both ways boards twice. At Rs25 a ride and 312 operating days, 800 daily boardings produce Rs6.24 million in annual fare revenue. If boardings halve, that revenue falls by Rs3.12 million, while much of the cost of owning the fleet remains. The model also assumes non-fare revenue at 37 percent of fares, which requires testing against actual advertising receipts. The 11 percent financing rate is an assumption rather than a financing commitment. Any interest subsidy must be funded and a guarantee can leave the state liable if repayments fail. Supporting 15,000 buses on those terms would cost around Rs240 billion a year. That is a recurring public expense. Pakistani households already spend an estimated Rs2.37 trillion a year on transport, according to the household survey. The question for the government is how much of that spending on a better service could save households and which trips people could make if the fare came down or the bus turned up regularly. Household savings cannot simply be netted against the government’s subsidy bill. A lower fare partly shifts costs from passengers to taxpayers — it does not eliminate them. Nor is all of the Rs2.37 trillion available to finance urban buses. The economic case must rest on savings in fuel and time, safer journeys and better access to work, alongside a credible plan for meeting the recurring budget commitment. WHAT THE POLICY NEEDS The policy can start by reconsidering the reported two percent development levy on buses and reviewing duties on electric buses and charging equipment. It can give affordable electric motorcycles and rickshaws greater priority in vehicle incentives. And it can make bus funding conditional on the service that provincial authorities and operators deliver. Localisation targets also need care. A rule designed around a petrol engine can penalise an electric motorcycle because its battery is imported. I would reward the value actually created in Pakistan, with a transition that allows battery and component suppliers to develop. The aim should be competitive suppliers that can sell beyond one protected domestic market. For bus funding, that means setting routes, fares and safety standards, then paying operators for running the scheduled service and maintaining the fleet. Provinces would have to pay on time and operators would have to run the promised service. Passengers should be able to see how often buses ran, how long they waited, and how many services were cancelled. Cities should also track who uses the system and ask people which journeys they still cannot make. A contract can make those obligations enforceable. The province could retain fare revenue and pay an operator for service delivered, with deductions for missed trips and safety failures. That reduces the incentive to overcrowd buses but leaves the province carrying the risk of weak ridership. Payment reserves and dependable budget releases would be necessary — private finance does not remove that obligation. Depots and power connections must be ready when the fleet arrives. I would begin with routes where demand can be tested, publish the results and expand where the service earns continued support. I would also want a travel survey to test the arguments made here. If low reported spending chiefly reflects short, affordable journeys and incomplete recall, the case for suppressed travel (when individuals do not undertake trips or activities due to barriers or constraints) would weaken. If well-run buses attract few riders, routes and spending should be reconsidered. A policy should allow those findings to change where the next rupee goes. Pakistan can keep a tally of cars coming off assembly lines. Over the next five years, it should also count how many more people can get to a job, a classroom or a clinic without buying a vehicle. For a woman making that journey, it comes down to what happens after the 20-minute walk: how long she waits, whether there’s room to get on and how much of her pay she has left when she gets home. The writer is a macroeconomist and professor of practice at IBA, Karachi. He can be reached at ammar.habib@gmail.com Published in Dawn, EOS, November 8th, 2026

items.title: Siblings acquitted in blasphemy case after 20 years
items.description: • SC sets aside death sentences upheld by LHC • Observes findings on mental illness raise doubts about culpability ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court on Saturday acquitted two brothers in a blasphemy case under Section 295-C of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), setting aside their death sentences earlier upheld by the Lahore High Court (LHC) over a decade ago. A three-judge SC bench, headed by Chief Justice of Pakistan Yahya Afridi and comprising Justices Shakeel Ahmad and Ishtiaq Ibrahim, took up criminal appeals against the Sept 17, 2015 decision of the LHC. The brothers, Liaqat Ali and Umar Draz, have spent around 20 years behind bars. They were convicted by a sessions judge in Jhang on March 27, 2006. The trial court sentenced both brothers to death and imposed a fine of Rs500,000 each, with five years’ rigorous imprisonment in default. The high court dismissed their appeals and upheld the convictions. The main SC judgement was authored by Justice Ishtiaq Ibrahim. Justice Shakeel Ahmad concurred with the order but also annexed an additional note. According to the complaint, Umar Draz had begun making explicit blasphemous statements, leading to a marital dispute between him and his wife that culminated in divorce on March 13, 2006. Draz explicitly affirmed in writing his conversion from Islam in the divorce papers. During the return of his former wife’s dowry articles, a written document auth­ored by co-appellant Liaqat Ali was recovered. It also contained blasphemous assertions. On March 18, 2006, when the complainant and witnesses confronted the brothers over the alleged blasphemous material, both appellants acknowledged and verified the contents of the documents and unequivocally declared their willingness to reiterate their assertions before any forum. Before the SC, their counsel confined his submissions to the plea of mental unsoundness, arguing that the appellants lacked the requisite mens rea (guilty mind) at the time of the alleged offence. The SC examined three psychiatric assessments. An initial three-member medical board at DHQ Hospital, Faisalabad, found both appellants mentally sound in 2007. However, an eight-member Board of Certification diagnosed them with “bipolar affective disorder with psychotic symptoms” in 2023. A nine-member Board of Certification in September 2025 concluded that both brothers were suffering from “bipolar disorder current episode manic”. It described the condition as a chronic illness that was most likely permanent in acute cases, with absent insight and an inability to understand their acts at the time. The SC observed that the unanimous opinions of specialised boards comprising senior professors of psychiatry carried greater weight than the earlier assessm­ent by a board with only one psychiatrist. It also noted that bipolar disorder was episodic and had a genetic component, and that both brothers had been independently diagnosed with the same condition. “The appellants have spent around 20 years behind bars. In the light of the opinion of medical board which raises doubts regarding the culpability of the appellants, the benefit of doubt cannot be withheld from the appellants,” the judgement said. While acquitting the appellants, the SC also expected the executive director of the Punjab Institute of Mental Health, Lahore, to ensure that their medical treatment was not discontinued. Additional note In his concurring note, Justice Ahmad agreed with the acquittal but cautioned that a psychiatric diagnosis alone did not satisfy the requirements of Section 84 of the PPC. The judge distinguished medical insanity from legal insanity, noting that the key question was whether, at the time of the offence, the accused was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law. He argued that legal accountability had to be balanced with humanity, explaining that true justice also included mercy when the law recognised a person’s lack of mental capacity. The note said the medical reports, along with the surrounding circumstances, created reasonable doubt. It also referred to Islamic principles of legal capacity and responsibility. Published in Dawn, November 8th, 2026

items.title: Un réseau de blanchiment tombe en Algérie : 50 millions DA, des devises et des armes saisis
items.description: L’Algérie poursuit sa guerre totale contre les réseaux de blanchiment d’argent . Les opérations spectaculaires se multiplient. La dernière en date a été menée samedi par les services de sécurité de l’Armée nationale populaire en 5ᵉ Région militaire (Constantine). Elle s’est soldée par le démantèlement d’un réseau criminel organisé spécialisé dans le blanchiment d’argent, la saisie d’importantes sommes d’argent en dinars et en euros, d’armes à feu ainsi que l’arrestation de 8 suspects. Blanchiment d’argent en Algérie : un réseau tombe dans l’Est du pays « Cette opération s’est soldée par l’arrestation de huit personnes et la saisie de sommes d’argent en monnaie nationale s’élevant à près de cinq milliards de centimes (50 millions de DA), ainsi que 45.125 euros et diverses sommes en devises étrangères. Aussi, il a été procédé à la saisie d’une quantité d’or estimée à 1,861 kilogramme, de huit véhicules touristiques et de quatre fusils de chasse, en sus d’autres effets utilisés dans des opérations de blanchiment d’argent », a indiqué le ministère de la Défense nationale dans un communiqué. Cette opération de « qualité confirme, une fois de plus, la mobilisation de l’ensemble des unités de l’Armée nationale populaire, afin de contrecarrer toutes les tentatives visant à porter atteinte à l’économie nationale », a ajouté la même source. L’Algérie a considérablement durci sa réglementation de lutte contre le blanchiment d’argent. En parallèle, les services de sécurité ont multiplié les opérations spectaculaires contre les réseaux de blanchiment et ont récupéré d’importantes sommes d’argent. L’article Un réseau de blanchiment tombe en Algérie : 50 millions DA, des devises et des armes saisis est apparu en premier sur TSA .
